Kookie
KOO-kee
adjective (Silent Generation slang)
From kook, an odd or crazy person, American slang of the late 1950s generally taken as a clipping of cuckoo (crazy, from the bird and its silly call). Kookie (also kooky) became a national word through the hip, comb-wielding parking-lot attendant nicknamed Kookie on television’s 77 Sunset Strip (from 1958), played by Edd Byrnes, and the 1959 novelty record "Kookie, Kookie (Lend Me Your Comb)."

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In 1959 kookie meant odd, eccentric, a little crazy — the fellow with the strange hobby, the girl with the wild hat, the neighbour who built a bomb shelter in the back yard. It was usually said with a grin, sometimes with a sneer. Scripture is honest that God’s people often look kookie to the world. When the Lord Jesus began His ministry, even His own friends said, "He is beside himself" (Mar 3:21). When Paul preached the resurrection before a Roman governor, Festus shouted, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad" (Act 26:24). Paul gladly owned the charge — he called himself a fool for Christ’s sake (1Co 4:10) — because "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27). So a Christian should be slow to call anyone kookie. The odd child in the classroom is "fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14), and he may be the one God has chosen. Grandchildren, there is a foolishness that is sin — the fool who says in his heart there is no God — and there is a foolishness that is faithfulness. If you follow Christ, someone will think you kookie. Wear it gladly, and never be the one who laughs at the odd kid at the lunch table.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (late 1950s, from kook, likely a clipping of cuckoo) for odd or crazy — a label the world pins on Christ’s people, for God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (1Co 1:27).

expand to see more

KOOKIE, adj. (Silent Generation slang, late 1950s; also kooky; from kook) Crazy, eccentric, odd. "Aunt Ruth’s got some kookie ideas about flying saucers."

Decode for families: odd or crazy; the world called Paul mad, and God chose the foolish things.

Key Scripture

Mar 3:21 — "And when his friends heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself."

Act 26:24 — "And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad."

1Co 4:10 — "We are fools for Christ's sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye are honourable, but we are despised."

1Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

Psa 139:14 — "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well."

Modern Corruption

Usually a playful word for eccentric, but it can become mockery of the odd and the weak, whom God has a habit of choosing.

expand to see more

Calling a friend’s idea kookie, with a smile, is no great sin, and a family that laughs at its own odd uncle with affection is a healthy one.

The word turns sharp when it is used to sort people into the normal and the strange, and to shut the strange ones out. That is the spirit of the crowd that called Jesus mad. Teach children that being odd is not the same as being wrong, and that being popular is not the same as being right.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French cucu → cuckoo (the bird; a fool) → late-1950s kook (an odd person) → kookie, kooky (crazy, eccentric).
